reference.source: ERS/ATS guidance and respiratory genetics texts
clinicalPearls: Presents with progressive exertional breathlessness and dry cough, often with hypoxaemia disproportionate to the physical examination
Hereditary disease from CSF2RA or CSF2RB mutations typically presents in childhood, unlike the commoner autoimmune (anti-GM-CSF antibody) form of adults
High-resolution imaging classically shows a crazy-paving pattern of ground-glass opacity with superimposed septal thickening
Bronchoalveolar lavage returns characteristically milky, opaque fluid rich in lipoproteinaceous material that stains positive with periodic acid-Schiff
Serum GM-CSF autoantibodies are absent in the hereditary form, and elevated serum GM-CSF levels point to receptor dysfunction
Whole-lung lavage is the mainstay for clearing accumulated material, and GM-CSF-directed strategies are used chiefly in the autoimmune form
Secondary infection, including with opportunistic organisms, can complicate the accumulated alveolar material
reference.pathophysiology: Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) signalling is essential for alveolar macrophages to mature and clear surfactant. In hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, biallelic mutations in CSF2RA or CSF2RB disrupt the GM-CSF receptor, so macrophages cannot catabolise surfactant despite abundant GM-CSF. Surfactant-derived lipoprotein therefore accumulates within the alveoli, impairing gas exchange and producing progressive restrictive lung disease and hypoxaemia. This contrasts with the autoimmune form, in which neutralising anti-GM-CSF antibodies block the same pathway.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary alveolar proteinosis from haematological disease or dust exposure
Other childhood interstitial lung diseases including surfactant disorders
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution chest computed tomography looking for crazy-paving
Bronchoalveolar lavage for characteristic milky fluid and periodic acid-Schiff staining
Serum anti-GM-CSF antibody assay to distinguish autoimmune from hereditary disease
Serum GM-CSF level and genetic testing of CSF2RA and CSF2RB
Pulmonary function tests showing a restrictive pattern with reduced gas transfer
Arterial blood gas or oximetry to quantify hypoxaemia
redFlags: Worsening hypoxaemia or respiratory failure requiring urgent whole-lung lavage
Superimposed infection with fever and clinical deterioration
Failure to thrive or exercise intolerance in an affected child
Development of pulmonary fibrosis on serial imaging
reference.prognosis: Whole-lung lavage can produce substantial symptomatic and physiological improvement, but hereditary disease often requires repeated procedures; long-term outcome depends on disease severity, response to lavage, and prevention of secondary infection and fibrosis.
pitfalls: Assuming all pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is autoimmune and omitting genetic testing in children
Mistaking crazy-paving for infection or pulmonary oedema and delaying diagnostic lavage
Overlooking secondary opportunistic infection when a stable patient deteriorates
Expecting a single lavage to be curative in the hereditary form
references: European Respiratory Society guidance on pulmonary alveolar proteinosis
management: Use whole-lung lavage as the mainstay to physically clear accumulated surfactant lipoprotein, accepting that repeated procedures are often required
Recognise that GM-CSF augmentation with inhaled or subcutaneous GM-CSF benefits the autoimmune form and is generally ineffective in receptor-defect hereditary disease
Provide supplemental oxygen and supportive care for hypoxaemia
Treat secondary respiratory infections promptly and maintain immunisation
Monitor with pulmonary function testing and gas transfer, oximetry and imaging to time repeat lavage
Consider lung transplantation for severe refractory disease, recognising the possibility of recurrence
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal recessive CSF2RA or CSF2RB receptor defect and family testing
